\(t_2 - t_1 = 4 - 2 = 2\), \(t_3 - t_2 = 6 - 4 = 2\), \(t_4 - t_3 = 8 - 6 = 2\).

The difference between consecutive terms is constant.

\(\therefore\) It is an A.P. with common difference \(d = 2\).

[Textbook note: the book prints the fourth term as \(\dfrac{7}{3}\); with that term the sequence is not an A.P., yet the printed answer key gives “Yes, \(d = \dfrac{1}{2}\)”, which holds only if the fourth term is \(\dfrac{7}{2}\). So the printed stem is a misprint for \(\dfrac{7}{2}\). The question is answered below exactly as printed, and the intended version is answered after it.]

**As printed.**

\(t_2 - t_1 = \dfrac{5}{2} - 2 = \dfrac{1}{2}\)

\(t_3 - t_2 = 3 - \dfrac{5}{2} = \dfrac{1}{2}\)

\(t_4 - t_3 = \dfrac{7}{3} - 3 = -\dfrac{2}{3}\)

\(\dfrac{1}{2} \neq -\dfrac{2}{3}\), so the difference is not constant.

\(\therefore\) As printed, the sequence is **not** an A.P.

**As intended** (fourth term \(\dfrac{7}{2}\)).

\(\dfrac{7}{2} - 3 = \dfrac{1}{2}\), so all three differences are \(\dfrac{1}{2}\).

\(\therefore\) It is an A.P. with \(d = \dfrac{1}{2}\), which is the printed answer.

Taking the terms exactly as printed, \(0.3\), \(0.33\), \(0.0333\):

\(t_2 - t_1 = 0.33 - 0.3 = 0.03\)

\(t_3 - t_2 = 0.0333 - 0.33 = -0.2967\)

The differences are not equal.

(The third term is almost certainly meant to be \(0.333\); even then \(0.333 - 0.33 = 0.003 \neq 0.03\), so the verdict is the same.)

\(\therefore\) The sequence is **not** an A.P.

Every term is \(-\dfrac{1}{5}\), so each difference is \(-\dfrac{1}{5} - \left(-\dfrac{1}{5}\right) = 0\).

A constant sequence is an A.P. whose common difference is zero.

\(\therefore\) It is an A.P. with \(d = 0\).

\(t_2 - t_1 = (3 + \sqrt{2}) - 3 = \sqrt{2}\)

\(t_3 - t_2 = (3 + 2\sqrt{2}) - (3 + \sqrt{2}) = \sqrt{2}\)

\(t_4 - t_3 = (3 + 3\sqrt{2}) - (3 + 2\sqrt{2}) = \sqrt{2}\)

\(\therefore\) It is an A.P. with common difference \(d = \sqrt{2}\).

(A common difference need not be rational — only constant.)

\(t_2 - t_1 = 132 - 127 = 5\), \(t_3 - t_2 = 137 - 132 = 5\).

\(\therefore\) It is an A.P. with common difference \(d = 5\).

In the A.P. 5, 1, -3, -7, the first term is the term written first.

\(\therefore\) \(a = 5\)

\(t_2 - t_1 = 1 - 5 = -4\)

\(t_3 - t_2 = -3 - 1 = -4\)

The difference is constant, so \(d = -4\).

\(\therefore\) First term \(a = 5\) and common difference \(d = -4\).

In the A.P. 0.6, 0.9, 1.2, 1.5, the first term is the term written first.

\(\therefore\) \(a = 0.6\)

\(t_2 - t_1 = 0.9 - 0.6 = 0.3\)

\(t_3 - t_2 = 1.2 - 0.9 = 0.3\)

The difference is constant, so \(d = 0.3\).

\(\therefore\) First term \(a = 0.6\) and common difference \(d = 0.3\).

In the A.P. 127, 135, 143, 151, the first term is the term written first.

\(\therefore\) \(a = 127\)

\(t_2 - t_1 = 135 - 127 = 8\)

\(t_3 - t_2 = 143 - 135 = 8\)

The difference is constant, so \(d = 8\).

\(\therefore\) First term \(a = 127\) and common difference \(d = 8\).

In the A.P. \(\dfrac{1}{4}, \dfrac{3}{4}, \dfrac{5}{4}, \dfrac{7}{4}\), the first term is the term written first.

\(\therefore\) \(a = \dfrac{1}{4}\)

\(t_2 - t_1 = \dfrac{3}{4} - \dfrac{1}{4} = \dfrac{2}{4} = \dfrac{1}{2}\)

\(t_3 - t_2 = \dfrac{5}{4} - \dfrac{3}{4} = \dfrac{1}{2}\)

The difference is constant, so \(d = \dfrac{1}{2}\).

\(\therefore\) First term \(a = \dfrac{1}{4}\) and common difference \(d = \dfrac{1}{2}\).

Note the boxes are printed out of order here; the terms themselves are

\(t_1 = -3\), \(t_2 = -8\), \(t_3 = -13\), \(t_4 = -18\),

\(t_2 - t_1 = -8 - (-3) = -5\), \(t_3 - t_2 = -13 - (-8) = -5\)

\(\therefore\) \(a = -3\), \(d = -5\)

The three digit natural numbers divisible by 5 are

100, 105, 110, . . . , 995.

(995 is the last, because the next multiple of 5 is 1000, which has four digits.)

This is an A.P. with \(a = 100\), \(d = 5\), \(t_n = 995\).

\(t_n = a + (n - 1)d\)

\(995 = 100 + (n - 1) \times 5\)

\(895 = 5(n - 1)\)

\(n - 1 = 179\)   \(\therefore\) \(n = 180\)

\(\therefore\) There are 180 three digit natural numbers divisible by 5.

The numbers from 10 to 250 divisible by 4 are

12, 16, 20, . . . , 248.

(12 is the first, because 10 and 11 are not multiples of 4; 248 is the last, because 252 exceeds 250.)

This is an A.P. with \(a = 12\), \(d = 4\), \(t_n = 248\).

\(t_n = a + (n - 1)d\)

\(248 = 12 + (n - 1) \times 4\)

\(236 = 4(n - 1)\)

\(n - 1 = 59\)   \(\therefore\) \(n = 60\)

\(\therefore\) 60 of them are divisible by 4.

Given \(t_{17} = t_{10} + 7\).

\(t_{17} = a + 16d\) and \(t_{10} = a + 9d\)

\(\therefore\) \(a + 16d = a + 9d + 7\)

\(\therefore\) \(7d = 7\)

\(\therefore\) \(d = 1\)

\(\therefore\) The common difference is 1. (Note \(a\) cancels, so it is not needed.)

The first 123 even natural numbers are 2, 4, 6, . . . , 246.

Here \(a = 2\), \(d = 2\), \(n = 123\), \(t_n = 2 \times 123 = 246\).

\(S_n = \dfrac{n}{2}(t_1 + t_n)\)

\(S_{123} = \dfrac{123}{2}(2 + 246) = \dfrac{123}{2} \times 248 = 123 \times 124 = 15252\)

\(\therefore\) The sum is 15252.

(The general result is \(n(n + 1)\), and \(123 \times 124 = 15252\) agrees.)

The even numbers **between** 1 and 350 are 2, 4, 6, . . . , 348 — 350 is excluded because the word “between” does not include the end value.

Here \(a = 2\), \(d = 2\), \(t_n = 348\).

\(t_n = a + (n - 1)d\)

\(348 = 2 + (n - 1)2\)   \(\therefore\) \(346 = 2(n - 1)\)   \(\therefore\) \(n = 174\)

\(S_n = \dfrac{n}{2}(t_1 + t_n)\)

\(S_{174} = \dfrac{174}{2}(2 + 348) = 87 \times 350 = 30450\)

\(\therefore\) The sum is 30450.

\(t_{19} = a + 18d = 52\) . . . (I)

\(t_{38} = a + 37d = 128\) . . . (II)

Subtracting (I) from (II): \(19d = 76\)   \(\therefore\) \(d = 4\)

From (I): \(a + 18 \times 4 = 52\)   \(\therefore\) \(a + 72 = 52\)   \(\therefore\) \(a = -20\)

\(S_n = \dfrac{n}{2}[2a + (n - 1)d]\)

\(S_{56} = \dfrac{56}{2}[2(-20) + (56 - 1) \times 4]\)

\(= 28[-40 + 220] = 28 \times 180 = 5040\)

\(\therefore\) The sum of the first 56 terms is 5040.

[Textbook note: the printed answer key lists this value under the label “5.” and prints no “4.” at all for Practice Set 3.3, so its numbering runs 1, 2, 3, 5, 5, 6, 7, 8. The value 5040 belongs to this question and 2380 to Q5; only the labels are wrong.]

\(S_{55} = 3300\), so with \(n = 55\)

\(S_n = \dfrac{n}{2}[2a + (n - 1)d]\)

\(3300 = \dfrac{55}{2}[2a + 54d]\)

\(3300 = 55[a + 27d]\)

\(a + 27d = \dfrac{3300}{55} = 60\)

But \(t_{28} = a + (28 - 1)d = a + 27d\).

\(\therefore\) \(t_{28} = 60\).

(\(a\) and \(d\) are not separately determined — only the combination \(a + 27d\) is, and that is exactly the \(28^{\text{th}}\) term, the middle term of the 55.)

Let the three consecutive terms be \(a - d\), \(a\), \(a + d\).

Sum: \((a - d) + a + (a + d) = 3a = 27\)   \(\therefore\) \(a = 9\)

Product: \((9 - d)(9)(9 + d) = 504\)

\(9(81 - d^2) = 504\)

\(81 - d^2 = 56\)

\(d^2 = 25\)   \(\therefore\) \(d = 5\) or \(d = -5\)

If \(d = 5\) the terms are 4, 9, 14; if \(d = -5\) they are 14, 9, 4.

Check: \(4 + 9 + 14 = 27\) and \(4 \times 9 \times 14 = 504\). \(\checkmark\)

\(\therefore\) The terms are 4, 9, 14 (or 14, 9, 4).

Let the four consecutive terms be \(a - d\), \(a\), \(a + d\), \(a + 2d\).

Sum: \(4a + 2d = 12\), i.e. \(2a + d = 6\) . . . (I)

\(3^{\text{rd}} + 4^{\text{th}}\): \((a + d) + (a + 2d) = 2a + 3d = 14\) . . . (II)

Subtracting (I) from (II): \(2d = 8\)   \(\therefore\) \(d = 4\)

From (I): \(2a + 4 = 6\)   \(\therefore\) \(a = 1\)

The terms are \(1 - 4 = -3\), \(1\), \(1 + 4 = 5\), \(1 + 8 = 9\).

Check: \(-3 + 1 + 5 + 9 = 12\) and \(5 + 9 = 14\). \(\checkmark\)

\(\therefore\) The four terms are \(-3\), 1, 5, 9.

Given \(t_9 = 0\), i.e. \(a + 8d = 0\), so \(a = -8d\).

\(t_{19} = a + 18d = -8d + 18d = 10d\)

\(t_{29} = a + 28d = -8d + 28d = 20d\)

\(\therefore\) \(t_{29} = 20d = 2 \times 10d = 2 \times t_{19}\)

\(\therefore\) The \(29^{\text{th}}\) term is twice the \(19^{\text{th}}\) term. Hence proved.

(Worth noticing: the result holds for every A.P. whose \(9^{\text{th}}\) term is zero — the proof never needs the value of \(a\) or \(d\) separately.)

Sanika saves \(\text{Rs. }10\) on 1 January, \(\text{Rs. }11\) on 2 January, \(\text{Rs. }12\) on 3 January, and so on — an A.P. with \(a = 10\), \(d = 1\).

**2016 is a leap year** (2016 is divisible by 4 and is not a century year), so from 1 January to 31 December there are \(n = 366\) days.

\(S_n = \dfrac{n}{2}[2a + (n - 1)d]\)

\(S_{366} = \dfrac{366}{2}[2 \times 10 + (366 - 1) \times 1]\)

\(= 183[20 + 365] = 183 \times 385 = 70455\)

\(\therefore\) Her total saving is \(\text{Rs. }70455\).

(Taking 365 days instead would give \(\text{Rs. }70080\), so the leap year matters.)

Total amount to be repaid \(= 8000 + 1360 = \text{Rs. }9360\), in \(n = 12\) instalments.

Each instalment is \(\text{Rs. }40\) less than the one before, so the instalments are in A.P. with \(d = -40\).

\(S_n = \dfrac{n}{2}[2a + (n - 1)d]\)

\(9360 = \dfrac{12}{2}[2a + (12 - 1)(-40)]\)

\(9360 = 6[2a - 440]\)

\(1560 = 2a - 440\)

\(2a = 2000\)   \(\therefore\) \(a = 1000\)

Last instalment \(= t_{12} = a + 11d = 1000 + 11(-40) = 1000 - 440 = 560\)

\(\therefore\) The first instalment is \(\text{Rs. }1000\) and the last is \(\text{Rs. }560\).

The seats per row are \(20, 22, 24, \ldots\) — an A.P. with \(a = 20\), \(d = 2\), and there are \(n = 27\) rows.

\(t_n = a + (n - 1)d\)

\(t_{15} = 20 + (15 - 1) \times 2 = 20 + 28 = 48\)

So the \(15^{\text{th}}\) row has 48 seats.

\(S_n = \dfrac{n}{2}[2a + (n - 1)d]\)

\(S_{27} = \dfrac{27}{2}[2 \times 20 + (27 - 1) \times 2] = \dfrac{27}{2}[40 + 52] = \dfrac{27}{2} \times 92 = 27 \times 46 = 1242\)

\(\therefore\) There are 48 seats in the \(15^{\text{th}}\) row and 1242 seats in the auditorium.

Let Monday's temperature be \(a\) and the common difference \(d\), so the six readings Monday to Saturday are \(t_1, t_2, \ldots, t_6\).

Given, as printed: (Monday + Saturday) is \(5^\circ\) more than (Tuesday + Saturday).

\(t_1 + t_6 = t_2 + t_6 + 5\)

Saturday appears on both sides and cancels:

\(t_1 = t_2 + 5\)   \(\therefore\) \(a = (a + d) + 5\)   \(\therefore\) \(d = -5\)

Wednesday is the third reading: \(t_3 = a + 2d = -30\)

\(a + 2(-5) = -30\)   \(\therefore\) \(a - 10 = -30\)   \(\therefore\) \(a = -20\)

So the six readings are

| Day | Mon | Tue | Wed | Thu | Fri | Sat |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Temperature (\(^\circ\)C) | -20 | -25 | -30 | -35 | -40 | -45 |

\(\therefore\) The other five days are \(-20^\circ\), \(-25^\circ\), \(-35^\circ\), \(-40^\circ\) and \(-45^\circ\) C (Wednesday being the given \(-30^\circ\) C).

The rows hold \(1, 2, 3, \ldots\) trees — an A.P. with \(a = 1\), \(d = 1\), \(n = 25\).

\(S_n = \dfrac{n}{2}[2a + (n - 1)d]\)

\(S_{25} = \dfrac{25}{2}[2 \times 1 + (25 - 1) \times 1] = \dfrac{25}{2}[2 + 24] = \dfrac{25}{2} \times 26 = 25 \times 13 = 325\)

\(\therefore\) 325 trees are planted in the 25 rows.

(This is the sum of the first 25 natural numbers, \(\dfrac{25 \times 26}{2} = 325\).)

The A.P. is \(-11, -8, -5, \ldots, 49\) with \(a = -11\), \(d = 3\).

Counting from the END, the terms are \(49\), \(49 - 3 = 46\), \(46 - 3 = 43\), \(43 - 3 = 40\).

\(\therefore\) The fourth term from the end is 40.

(Equivalently: reverse the A.P., so \(a' = 49\), \(d' = -3\), and \(t_4' = 49 + 3(-3) = 40\).)

Here \(a = -5\), last term \(t_n = 45\) and \(S_n = 120\).

Use the form that needs only the two end terms:

\(S_n = \dfrac{n}{2}(t_1 + t_n)\)

\(120 = \dfrac{n}{2}(-5 + 45) = \dfrac{n}{2} \times 40 = 20n\)

\(\therefore\) \(n = 6\)

Now use \(t_n = a + (n - 1)d\) with \(n = 6\):

\(45 = -5 + 5d\)   \(\therefore\) \(5d = 50\)   \(\therefore\) \(d = 10\)

\(\therefore\) There are 6 terms and the common difference is 10 (the A.P. is \(-5, 5, 15, 25, 35, 45\)).

The sum of the first \(n\) natural numbers is \(\dfrac{n(n + 1)}{2}\).

\(\dfrac{n(n + 1)}{2} = 36\)

\(n(n + 1) = 72\)

\(n^2 + n - 72 = 0\)

\((n + 9)(n - 8) = 0\)   \(\therefore\) \(n = -9\) or \(n = 8\)

\(n\) is a count of terms, so it must be a natural number and \(n = -9\) is rejected.

\(\therefore\) \(n = 8\). (Check: \(1 + 2 + \cdots + 8 = 36\).)

Let the three parts be \(a - d\), \(a\), \(a + d\).

Sum: \((a - d) + a + (a + d) = 3a = 207\)   \(\therefore\) \(a = 69\)

Taking \(d > 0\), the two smaller parts are \(a - d\) and \(a\).

Product: \((69 - d) \times 69 = 4623\)

\(69 - d = \dfrac{4623}{69} = 67\)   \(\therefore\) \(d = 2\)

\(\therefore\) The three parts are 67, 69 and 71.

Check: \(67 + 69 + 71 = 207\) and \(67 \times 69 = 4623\). \(\checkmark\)

With 37 terms, the three terms exactly in the middle are \(t_{18}, t_{19}, t_{20}\) (18 terms before them and 18 after).

Their sum \(= 3t_{19} = 225\)   \(\therefore\) \(t_{19} = a + 18d = 75\) . . . (I)

The last three terms are \(t_{35}, t_{36}, t_{37}\), whose sum \(= 3t_{36} = 429\)

\(\therefore\) \(t_{36} = a + 35d = 143\) . . . (II)

Subtracting (I) from (II): \(17d = 68\)   \(\therefore\) \(d = 4\)

From (I): \(a + 72 = 75\)   \(\therefore\) \(a = 3\)

Last term \(t_{37} = 3 + 36 \times 4 = 147\).

\(\therefore\) The A.P. is \(3, 7, 11, \ldots, 147\).

(Both shortcuts used the same fact: in any A.P. the sum of three consecutive terms is three times the middle one.)

Let the A.P. have first term \(a\), second term \(b\) and \(n\) terms in all, the last being \(c\).

Common difference \(d = b - a\).

Last term: \(c = a + (n - 1)d = a + (n - 1)(b - a)\)

\(\therefore\) \(n - 1 = \dfrac{c - a}{b - a}\)   \(\therefore\) \(n = \dfrac{c - a}{b - a} + 1 = \dfrac{c - a + b - a}{b - a} = \dfrac{b + c - 2a}{b - a}\)

Now use the first-plus-last form of the sum:

\(S_n = \dfrac{n}{2}(\text{first term} + \text{last term}) = \dfrac{n}{2}(a + c)\)

Substituting \(n\):

\(S_n = \dfrac{1}{2} \times \dfrac{b + c - 2a}{b - a} \times (a + c) = \dfrac{(a + c)(b + c - 2a)}{2(b - a)}\)

Hence proved. (\(b \neq a\) is needed, i.e. the common difference is not zero.)

Let the A.P. have first term \(a\) and common difference \(d\).

\(S_p = \dfrac{p}{2}[2a + (p - 1)d]\) and \(S_q = \dfrac{q}{2}[2a + (q - 1)d]\)

Given \(S_p = S_q\):

\(\dfrac{p}{2}[2a + (p - 1)d] = \dfrac{q}{2}[2a + (q - 1)d]\)

\(2a(p - q) + d[p(p - 1) - q(q - 1)] = 0\)

\(p(p - 1) - q(q - 1) = p^2 - q^2 - (p - q) = (p - q)(p + q - 1)\)

\(\therefore\) \((p - q)\{2a + (p + q - 1)d\} = 0\)

Since \(p \neq q\), \(p - q \neq 0\), so

\(2a + (p + q - 1)d = 0\) . . . (I)

Now

\(S_{p+q} = \dfrac{p + q}{2}[2a + (p + q - 1)d] = \dfrac{p + q}{2} \times 0 = 0\)

Hence the sum of the first \((p + q)\) terms is zero. Hence proved.

Let the A.P. have first term \(a\) and common difference \(d\), so \(t_m = a + (m - 1)d\) and \(t_n = a + (n - 1)d\).

Given \(m\,t_m = n\,t_n\):

\(m[a + (m - 1)d] = n[a + (n - 1)d]\)

\(a(m - n) + d[m(m - 1) - n(n - 1)] = 0\)

\(m(m - 1) - n(n - 1) = m^2 - n^2 - (m - n) = (m - n)(m + n - 1)\)

\(\therefore\) \((m - n)\{a + (m + n - 1)d\} = 0\)

For the statement to have content \(m \neq n\), so \(m - n \neq 0\) and

\(a + (m + n - 1)d = 0\)

But \(t_{m+n} = a + (m + n - 1)d\).

\(\therefore\) \(t_{m+n} = 0\), i.e. the \((m + n)^{\text{th}}\) term is zero. Hence proved.

Simple interest \(= \dfrac{P \times R \times N}{100}\) with \(P = 1000\) and \(R = 10\).

Simple interest after 1 year \(= \dfrac{1000 \times 10 \times 1}{100} = 100\)

Simple interest after 2 years \(= \dfrac{1000 \times 10 \times 2}{100} = 200\)

Simple interest after 3 years \(= \dfrac{1000 \times 10 \times 3}{100} = 300\)

According to this the simple interest for 4, 5, 6 years will be 400, **500**, **600** respectively.

The totals \(100, 200, 300, 400, \ldots\) have a constant difference of 100, so they are in A.P.

From this \(d = 100\) and \(a = 100\).

Amount of simple interest after 20 years:

\(t_n = a + (n - 1)d\)

\(t_{20} = 100 + (20 - 1) \times 100\)

\(t_{20} = 100 + 1900 = 2000\)

\(\therefore\) The amount of simple interest after 20 years is \(\text{Rs. }2000\).

(Directly: \(\dfrac{1000 \times 10 \times 20}{100} = 2000\), which agrees.)
